title: 3SUM: all triples vs sorting with two pointers
problem_statement: Given n integers a_1..a_n, decide whether there are indices i < j < k with a_i + a_j + a_k = 0.

input.size_measure: n machine words (values bounded by O(n^2) in the harness).

algorithms.name: all triples
algorithms.pseudocode: for i < j < k: if a_i + a_j + a_k = 0: yes
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n^3) worst case: exactly C(n, 3) equality tests and C(n, 2) target computations on every no-instance, at most that on every input (PROOFS.md section 1)
algorithms.correctness: Exhaustive: every triple i < j < k is tested (PROOFS.md section 1).

algorithms.name: sort + two pointers
algorithms.idea: Sort. For each i, move pointers j (from the left) and k (from the right) over a[i+1..n-1] toward each other, depending on the sign of the sum.
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n^2) in the worst case, assuming the built-in sort runs in O(n log n) (machine-model assumption, listed under background; any O(n^2) bound would do): exactly (n - 1)(n - 2)/2 pointer steps on every no-instance with n >= 1 (none for n = 0) and at most that on every input, plus the sort of the n values (PROOFS.md section 2)
algorithms.space_complexity: Theta(n) under the same assumption: the sorted copy (n slots) and the built-in sort's working space, which the assumption takes to be O(n) (PROOFS.md section 2)
algorithms.correctness: For fixed i the pair sums a[j] + a[k] are monotone in j and k on the sorted array, so the two-pointer scan never skips a solution: no solution pair lies outside the current window [j, k] (complete proof: PROOFS.md section 2).

relationship: Theta(n^3) -> Theta(n^2) in the worst case, the quadratic bound assuming the built-in sort runs in O(n log n) (background), so the T3 tag rests on that assumption (PROOFS.md sections 1-3). The 3SUM conjectures and the known subquadratic and decision-tree results are listed under background; this entry proves no lower bound for 3SUM.

sources.title: Objects/listsort.txt: the description of CPython's list sort
sources.note: Background only. The file dates from 2002 (T. Peters); the cited passage, which states that the code uses the powersort merge strategy of Munro and Wild, is a later addition. Read in the current version of the main branch on 2026-10-07.

verification.method: V1: both agree with each other and with an independent hash-based oracle on random instances with values in [-n^2, n^2] (yes and no answers both occur), n = 0..60 for the cubic algorithm. V2: worst-case instances (all values positive, so no solution and no early exit; PROOFS.md section 4) fitted against n^3 and n^2 (timing, measured). Proofs: PROOFS.md proves the correctness, the exact step counts on no-instances, the worst-case bounds and the space of both algorithms (the quadratic algorithm's upper bounds under the machine-model assumption on the built-in sort), and names their deterministic checks (tests/test_proofs_three_sum.py).

caveats: The 3SUM conjecture for integer inputs (3SUM needs n^(2-o(1)) time; background) is a hypothesis, not a theorem; its Omega(n^2) form is false (background); and this entry proves no lower bound for 3SUM. Both bounds are worst cases: on a yes-instance either algorithm can stop at its first solution.

background.statement: A large class of problems in computational geometry is at least as difficult as 3SUM (3SUM-hard); this proves no lower bound for them, but there is no hope of o(n^2) algorithms for them unless the solution for 3SUM can be improved; the best known algorithm for 3SUM then took Theta(n^2) time.

The conjecture that 3SUM needs Omega(n^2) time is false: 3SUM has a deterministic O(n^2 / (log n / log log n)^(2/3)) algorithm and decision-tree complexity O(n^(3/2) sqrt(log n)). For integer inputs it is conjectured that 3SUM needs n^(2-o(1)) time, i.e. that no O(n^(2-eps)) algorithm exists for any eps > 0.

For every constant k, k-SUM on n elements can be solved by linear decision trees with O(n log^2 n) linear queries, which are comparison queries (they compare the sums of two k-subsets); so no quadratic lower bound can be proved in that model.

Machine-model assumption of this entry: the built-in sort (sorted() and list.sort()) runs in O(n log n) comparisons and time, with O(n) extra space, in the worst case on n items. Basis, as far as the sources go: the current CPython list sort orders its merges by the powersort rule of Munro and Wild (listsort.txt), and with a plain merge powersort makes at most n H + 3n - r <= n log2 n + 3n comparisons on n items forming r runs, where H is the entropy of the run lengths (Munro & Wild 2018, Theorem 6 of the arXiv version). CPython's merges also gallop, which that theorem does not cover, so the assumption is not proved in this repository.
background.source: Munro & Wild 2018, Theorem 6 (arXiv version), for the plain-merge bound; Python Software Foundation, Objects/listsort.txt, for the merge order of the current CPython list sort
